page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: BF₃ is electron deficient
lines: Three shared pairs give boron only six
electrons in its valence shell, which is
So BF₃ is an electron deficient molecule.
steps.why: The Lewis acid behaviour of BF₃ rests on the electron count at boron, so the count has to be done first: three shared pairs are six electrons, not eight.
common_mistakes: Counting the lone pairs on the fluorine atoms as part of the octet of boron. Only the three shared pairs belong to boron.
Writing that BF₃ gives H⁺. It has no hydrogen; it is an acid in the Lewis sense only.
steps.memory_tip: Three bonds, six electrons. Two short of eight is what makes boron an acceptor.
steps.margin_note: The count six electrons, two short of an octet is the line to write here.

steps.label: It accepts a lone pair
lines: A Lewis acid is a substance that accepts
The empty 2p orbital of boron accepts a
lone pair from a donor such as NH₃, and
steps.why: The definition of a Lewis acid is about accepting a lone pair, so the answer is complete only when the acceptance is shown. The ammonia adduct is the standard example: the nitrogen lone pair fills the empty orbital on boron.
common_mistakes: Defining a Lewis acid as a proton donor. That is the Bronsted definition.
Writing that BF₃ donates a lone pair. It accepts one; the donor is the base.
steps.memory_tip: An acid accepts, a base donates. BF₃ has the empty orbital, so BF₃ accepts.
steps.margin_note: One adduct such as BF₃·NH₃ shows the acceptance in writing.

insider_note: The electron count at boron and the definition of a Lewis acid are two separate statements, and the answer needs both of them.
